title: Tenant preemptive safety profiles for reserved capacity and burst handling
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: PRD for a tenant-level 'safety profile' system that defines how reserved capacity behaves under contention: preemption thresholds, grace credits, soft-evict windows, and burst fallback policies. The goal is predictable isolation for paying tenants while enabling safe transient bursts and graceful degradation across Dedicated pools.
context: Operations teams have observed tenant contention at tail events where low-latency customers experience degraded SLOs when noisy tenants trigger large transient bursts. Existing reserve and burst mechanisms are coarse-grained. This initiative builds configurable profiles that encode tenant expectations and enable automated, auditable preemption decisions that work with autoscaling and routing layers.
objectives: 1) Provide a per-tenant profile that specifies preemption aggressiveness, burst grace, and preferred fallback strategies. 2) Ensure predictable latency for high-SLA tenants even during zone-level pressure. 3) Integrate with existing autoscaling and soft-evict mechanisms so profiles can be enforced without manual intervention. 4) Expose audit logs and explainability for preemption actions to support customer questions and appeals.
non_goals: 1) This PRD does not change low-level scheduling kernels or GPU affinity heuristics. 2) It does not replace billing or entitlement logic — profiles are policy only. 3) Does not implement a marketplace for buying ad-hoc burst credits in this phase.
user_stories: As a platform SRE, I want to assign an aggressive safety profile to a high-SLA tenant so their requests are preempted last during contention.
As a tenant admin, I want to set a 5-minute burst grace period so short traffic spikes are absorbed without evictions.
As an on-call engineer, I want preemption decisions to include an explainability token and link to the event so I can triage customer escalations.
As a product manager, I want telemetry that correlates preemption events with customer errors and cost so we can refine profiles.
As a privacy officer, I want profiles to be auditable without leaking request payloads, linked only by request IDs and anonymized metrics.
solution_overview: Introduce a Safety Profile CRD (policy object) stored in the control plane and enforced by the capacity orchestration layer. Profiles include: priority_weight (numeric), burst_grace_seconds, soft_evict_window_seconds, preempt_score_threshold, fallback_strategy (run-on-host|route-to-hosted|queue), and credit_bucket_id. The orchestration engine uses profile parameters to compute a preemption score combining tenant weight, recent burst history, and available grace credits. If score exceeds threshold, the engine triggers policy actions (soft-evict, routed fallback, or preempt) with accompanying audit metadata.
architecture_notes:
- Profiles stored in Private control plane with RBAC and KMS-encrypted fields for credit_bucket references.
- Orchestrator module will compute preemption_score = f(priority_weight, burst_rate, grace_remaining, pool_pressure).
- Integration points: capacity allocator, autoscaler, routing policy, console UI, and logs pipeline (structured events).
- Minimal changes to runtime: runtime receives eviction intent with request tags; runtime can checkpoint warm KV cache for tenants marked as 'preempt-resume' to support fast restore.
performance_criteria: 1) High-SLA tenants with aggressive profiles should maintain 99th percentile latency degradation <= 10% under moderate transient pressure (simulated 2x baseline load). 2) Preemption decision latency (time from decision to action) <= 2s for soft-evict actions. 3) System must not increase baseline CPU usage on control plane orchestration by more than 5% at 95th percentile during decision windows.
security_considerations:
- Profiles are a policy surface; ensure only authorized users can create aggressive profiles.
- Audit logs must be tamper-evident; pipeline writes immutable entries to our logging store with retention policy.
- credit_bucket references may map to billing entitlements; ensure encryption in transit and at rest.
- Expose minimal explainability fields in customer-facing logs to avoid data leakage.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): implement read-only UI and evaluation mode where profile recommendations are suggested but not enforced; run for 4 weeks across 5% of tenants. Phase 2 (soft-enforce): enable orchestration to take soft-evict actions for a subset of non-critical pools with safety limits. Phase 3 (full enforce): enable preemptive evictions and routing fallbacks for production pools with monitoring and rollback targets. Each phase includes a 2-week observation window and an on-call playbook.
monitoring_and_alerting:
- New metrics: preemption_count_by_tenant, preemption_latency_ms, grace_credit_balance, profile_trigger_rate.
- Dashboards: per-pool and per-tenant preemption heatmaps, runbook links.
- Alerts: high preemption_rate OR unexplained error spikes correlated with preemption actions triggers severity P0 page to capacity-oncall.
- Audit trail: every preemption decision writes an event containing tenant_id, profile_id, reason_code, and correlation_id.
acceptance_criteria: A1: Safety profile schema implemented in control plane and editable by RBAC-authorized users through Console and API.
A2: Orchestration uses profile parameters to compute preemption decisions in evaluation mode with logs for every simulated decision.
A3: Canary rollout across at least 5 production tenants without an increase in P99 errors for their high-SLA routes beyond threshold defined in performance_criteria.
A4: Soft-evict actions complete within 2s in >=95% of test runs in lab and can be traced from decision -> action -> audit event in logs.
A5: Console shows profile attribution in tenant cost/latency dashboard and exposes explainability token for each preemption event.
A6: Security review completed and sign-off obtained from InfoSec; audit pipeline tested with tamper detection and access controls.
A7: Integration tests verifying profile interaction with autoscaler and fallback routing exist and pass in CI with synthetic pressure tests.
open_questions: Q1: Should profiles permit negative priority_weight to represent tenants that must be evicted before best-effort workloads?
Q2: What is the default grace_credit replenishment rate for burst credits (fixed per hour or adaptive based on steady-state usage)?
Q3: How should billing interact with credit buckets for customers that run out of credits mid-burst? Immediate throttle, queued requests, or fallback to hosted?
Q4: Do we expose profile analytics to customers or only to account owners/admins?
Q5: Is there a need for profile templating (gold/silver/bronze) for fast onboarding?
decisions: D1: Use numeric priority_weight (0-100) instead of enumerated tiers to allow fine-grained ordering.
D2: Implement grace credits as integer tokens that decrement on burst consumption and replenish at a configurable rate per tenant bucket.
D3: Fallback strategies supported initially: route-to-hosted and queue-with-timeout; run-on-host fallback deferred to later phase.
notes: Early design critiques from runtime and infra teams raised concerns about request tagging overhead; we will prototype with lightweight tags and measure. Action: ENG to provide cost estimate for tag propagation by 2025-02-18. Also coordinate with Billing for credit_bucket mapping.
